title: Prefix sums and matrices
description: Range sums in O(1), counting subarrays with a running total and a map, range updates with difference arrays, and the classic grid walks.

challenges.title: Range Sum Queries
challenges.prompt:
Given an integer list `nums` and a list of `queries`, where each query `[left, right]` asks for the sum of `nums[left]` through `nums[right]` inclusive, return the answers in order.

There can be as many queries as numbers, so adding up each range from scratch is O(n) per query. Do O(n) preparation once and answer every query in O(1).

examples.explain: 3 - 1 + 4 = 6, then -1 + 4 + 1 - 5 = -1, then the single value 1, then the whole list.

hints: Precompute `prefix[i]`, the sum of the first i numbers, with `prefix[0] = 0`.
The sum from left to right inclusive is `prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left]`. The extra leading 0 means a range that starts at index 0 needs no special case.
challenges.explanation: prefix[i] holds the sum of nums[0..i-1], so the sum of nums[left..right] is everything up to right minus everything before left: prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left]. Building the list is one O(n) pass and each query is one subtraction. Making the list one longer than nums, with a leading 0, removes the special case for ranges that start at index 0.

challenges.title: Count Subarrays That Sum to k
challenges.pattern: Prefix sums plus a hash map
challenges.prompt: Given an integer list `nums` and an integer `k`, return how many contiguous, non-empty subarrays add up to exactly `k`. The values can be negative or zero, so a sliding window will not work. Aim for O(n).

examples.explain: [3, -3] twice, [-3, 3] once, and the whole list.

hints: A subarray from i to j sums to `prefix(j) - prefix(i - 1)`. So a subarray ending here sums to k exactly when an earlier running total equals `running - k`.
Keep a map from each running total to how many times it has appeared so far. At every step, add `count[running - k]` to the answer, then record `running`.
Seed the map with `{0: 1}`: the empty prefix lets subarrays that start at index 0 be counted.

solution.python:
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    seen = {0: 1}                       # running total -> how many times seen
    running = 0
    count = 0
    for x in nums:
        running += x
        count += seen.get(running - k, 0)   # earlier totals that leave exactly k
        seen[running] = seen.get(running, 0) + 1
    return count

challenges.explanation: Each subarray is the difference of two prefix totals. Walking left to right, the subarrays ending at the current index that sum to k correspond one to one with earlier prefix totals equal to running - k, and the map counts those in O(1). Look up before recording the current total so a subarray is never empty. A sliding window fails here because adding a negative number can shrink the sum, so a window that is too big can become valid again.

challenges.title: Apply Range Increments
challenges.prompt:
Start with a list of `n` zeros. Each entry of `updates` is `[start, end, delta]`: add `delta` to every position from `start` to `end` inclusive. Return the list after all of the updates.

Applying each update position by position costs O(n) per update. Aim for O(n + u) in total for u updates.
hints: Do not touch every position. Record only where each change starts and where it stops.
Keep a difference list `diff` of length n + 1. For `[start, end, delta]` do `diff[start] += delta` and `diff[end + 1] -= delta`.
A running sum over `diff` turns those marks back into the final values: the running total at position i is the result for i.

solution.python:
def apply_increments(n, updates):
    diff = [0] * (n + 1)
    for start, end, delta in updates:
        diff[start] += delta            # the change begins here
        diff[end + 1] -= delta          # and stops after end
    out = []
    running = 0
    for i in range(n):
        running += diff[i]
        out.append(running)
    return out

challenges.explanation: A difference list stores how much each position differs from the one before it. A range update changes only two of those differences: +delta where the range starts and -delta just after it ends. A prefix sum over the differences rebuilds the values. The extra slot at index n absorbs updates that end on the last position.

challenges.title: Rectangle Sums in a Grid
challenges.prompt:
Given a grid of integers `matrix` and a list of `queries`, each `[r1, c1, r2, c2]` naming the top-left cell `(r1, c1)` and the bottom-right cell `(r2, c2)` of a rectangle, return the sum of the values inside each rectangle, in order.

Prepare in O(rows * cols) so that every query takes O(1).

examples.explain: The top-left 2 x 2 block is 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 12, and the bottom row is 7 + 8 + 9 = 24.

constraints: 0 <= r1 <= r2 < rows and 0 <= c1 <= c2 < cols
hints: Build `P` with one extra row and column of zeros, where `P[r + 1][c + 1]` is the sum of the rectangle from (0, 0) to (r, c).
Fill it with inclusion and exclusion: `P[r + 1][c + 1] = matrix[r][c] + P[r][c + 1] + P[r + 1][c] - P[r][c]`. The top-left block was added twice, so subtract it once.
A query is the big rectangle minus the strip above and the strip to the left, plus the corner that was removed twice: `P[r2 + 1][c2 + 1] - P[r1][c2 + 1] - P[r2 + 1][c1] + P[r1][c1]`.
challenges.explanation: The 2D prefix table stores the sum of every block anchored at the top-left corner. Building a cell adds the block above and the block to the left, which counts their overlap twice, so the overlap is subtracted once. A query uses the same inclusion and exclusion in reverse: four table reads per rectangle. The padding row and column of zeros remove every special case for rectangles that touch the top or left edge.

challenges.title: Spiral Order
challenges.prompt: Given a grid `matrix` with `rows` rows and `cols` columns, return all of its values in spiral order: start at the top-left corner, go right along the top row, down the right column, left along the bottom row and up the left column, then keep circling inward until every value has been listed exactly once.

examples.explain: One full lap, then the center.
The inner layer is the single row 6, 7, which is walked only once.

hints: Track four boundaries: `top`, `bottom`, `left` and `right`. Each lap walks the outer layer and then pulls those boundaries inward.
Walk the top row and do `top += 1`, walk the right column and do `right -= 1`, then the bottom row and the left column the same way.
Thin grids are the trap. Before walking the bottom row check `top <= bottom`, and before walking the left column check `left <= right`, or a single remaining row or column is listed twice.

solution.python:
def spiral_order(matrix):
    out = []
    top, bottom = 0, len(matrix) - 1
    left, right = 0, len(matrix[0]) - 1
    while top <= bottom and left <= right:
        for c in range(left, right + 1):        # top row, left to right
            out.append(matrix[top][c])
        top += 1
        for r in range(top, bottom + 1):        # right column, downward
            out.append(matrix[r][right])
        right -= 1
        if top <= bottom:                       # bottom row, right to left
            for c in range(right, left - 1, -1):
                out.append(matrix[bottom][c])
            bottom -= 1
        if left <= right:                       # left column, upward
            for r in range(bottom, top - 1, -1):
                out.append(matrix[r][left])
            left += 1
    return out

challenges.explanation: Four boundaries describe the unvisited layer. Each side is walked once and its boundary moves inward right after, so nothing is visited twice. The two extra checks matter when the remaining area is a single row or a single column: after the top row and right column are taken, there may be no bottom row or left column left to walk. Another valid approach steps in one direction and turns right whenever the next cell is outside the grid or already visited.

challenges.title: Rotate an Image
challenges.prompt: An image is stored as an `n x n` grid `matrix`. Rotate it 90 degrees clockwise **in place**: change the values inside `matrix` itself instead of building a second grid. Return `matrix` when you are done so the tests can check it.

examples.explain: The first column, read from the bottom up, becomes the first row.

hints: Look at where row 0 ends up: it becomes the last column. Two simple in-place moves combine into that.
Transpose first: swap `matrix[r][c]` with `matrix[c][r]` for every `c > r`, so rows become columns.
Then reverse each row. Transpose plus reverse rows is a clockwise turn; transpose plus reverse columns would turn it counterclockwise.
challenges.explanation: A clockwise turn sends the value at (r, c) to (c, n - 1 - r). Transposing sends (r, c) to (c, r), and reversing each row then sends (c, r) to (c, n - 1 - r), so the two steps together are exactly the rotation, using O(1) extra space. Swapping only above the diagonal matters: looping over every pair would swap each one twice and undo the transpose.

challenges.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
challenges.prompt: Given a grid `matrix`, find every cell that holds `0` and set the whole row and the whole column of that cell to `0`. Only zeros that were in the original grid count: a zero you write must not wipe out further rows and columns. Change `matrix` in place and return it.

examples.explain: Rows 1 and 2 and columns 1 and 3 are cleared. Only the original two zeros count.

hints: If you write zeros while you scan, a new zero looks exactly like an original one and wipes out rows it should not. Find first, write second.
First pass: record which rows and which columns contain a zero, in two sets or two boolean lists.
Second pass: set a cell to 0 when its row or its column was recorded. For O(1) extra space, the follow-up stores those marks in row 0 and column 0 themselves, plus one flag for column 0.
challenges.explanation: Separating the scan from the writes is what keeps written zeros from spreading. The first pass remembers which rows and columns to clear, the second pass clears them. This uses O(rows + cols) extra space. The classic follow-up gets O(1) space by keeping those marks in the first row and first column of the grid itself, with one extra flag because cell (0, 0) cannot mark both its row and its column.
